case.lead: An open web platform to digitize, compare and share historical maps in the classroom.

meta.clientV: A history and geography teacher and a university lecturer

problem.title: The problem
problem.p: History and geography teachers work with old maps that are overloaded, often incomplete, hard to compare over time and shared in a disorganized way.

extract.d: Upload a map, extract its text, colors and shapes, then place them on a standardized world map.

edit.d: Filter, edit or enrich the elements to fit the lesson's goals.

time.d: Attach dates to maps to see how a territory evolved.

lib.d: Share and discover maps from other teachers.

case.shot1: A 1775 map digitized in Atlas (left), next to the original (right).
case.shot2: How the territory evolved from 1783 to 1800, using the timeline.

mgmt.d: Product backlog and sprints in Jira, task breakdown based on dependencies between the web platform and the extraction modules, deadline tracking and a weekly dashboard.

shapes.d: Designed and built the module that extracts shapes from a map (arrows, territories, symbols), from the picker in the Vue interface to the Celery task in Python and OpenCV.

deploy.d: Put Atlas online on Oracle Cloud for $0 per month, over HTTPS, with a one-command deployment script, backups and rollback.

shapes.title: Deep dive: shape extraction
shapes.p1: Our first pipeline was fully automatic, but old maps are very noisy: rivers, coastlines, text and hatching all turned into unwanted shapes. On a 1775 map where we expected 3 arrows, it found 28, and users had to delete the rest by hand.
shapes.p2: I compared three approaches: refining the automatic pipeline, integrating an AI segmentation model (MobileSAM), or letting users click the shapes they want. I chose the third, which was presented to and approved by the client: one click per shape, then color segmentation in the CIE LAB space with two thresholds (hysteresis) to capture soft edges without spilling into neighboring regions.
shapes.p3: The solution is covered by regression tests (pytest) that simulate one click per reference shape and require an IoU above 0.9.

deploy.title: Deep dive: deployment
deploy.p1: Atlas runs about a dozen Docker services (FastAPI, Vue, PostGIS, Redis, Celery and AI workers, Keycloak). The challenge: make it available to the client at no cost, securely, and easy to redeploy.
deploy.list:
• $0 per month on an Oracle Cloud Always Free ARM instance (4 cores, 24 GB).
  • A single HTTPS entry point through the Caddy proxy and Let's Encrypt, instead of four exposed HTTP ports.
  • Generated secrets, non-root containers, admin console restricted to specific IP addresses.
  • One command (deploy.sh): setup, firewall, migrations, database backup and a health check on every service.
  • Rollback (rollback.sh) to the last working version, with no data loss.

learn.title: What I took away
learn.p1: Atlas confirmed that I enjoy coordinating as much as developing: a well-written ticket and anticipated dependencies save the whole team time.
learn.p2: It also taught me to hold my own tasks to the standard I ask of others. I pushed my first version of shape extraction too long before changing approach. Now I set measurable acceptance criteria and a checkpoint before committing to a solution.
